title: Trembling and astonishment (Mark 16:1–8)
hook: the women find the tomb empty; the oldest copies end with them fleeing, afraid

segments.voice: Yesterday, a council member who dared to ask for the body, Joseph, and your line was he went in boldly.

The Sabbath is over. Very early on Sunday, as the sun comes up, three women walk to the tomb: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. They've bought spices to anoint his body, the last thing they can do for him. On the way they worry about something very practical: who will roll away the stone for us? Mark says it was very great. Two of them had seen where he was laid. Then they look up. The stone is already rolled back.
screen: `VERY EARLY, THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` → `WHO WILL ROLL AWAY THE STONE?` → `IT'S ALREADY ROLLED BACK.`

segments.voice: They go into the tomb, and sitting on the right side is a young man in a long white robe. They are terrified. He says, in the King James Bible: "Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him." Then a message: go, tell his disciples, and Peter, that he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he said. And Peter. Of all the names to single out, the one who denied him three times by the fire. Then comes the last verse of Mark in the oldest complete copies: "And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid." That's it. No appearance of the risen Jesus. No reunion. Just women running from an empty tomb, shaking. In Greek the sentence ends, literally, they were afraid, for: on a small word, gar, like a sentence cut off mid-breath. Scholars still argue about it. Maybe the last page was lost. Maybe Mark meant to stop here. If he did, the ending is a kind of invitation: the story isn't finished; it hands the next step to whoever is reading. And the women can't have stayed silent forever, or there'd be no story to read. Mark leaves them in trembling and astonishment: not calm, not neat, but awe. Trembling is tromos; astonishment is ekstasis, a word for being beside yourself, something so big it takes a person outside themselves.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN IN A WHITE ROBE.` · `TELL HIS DISCIPLES, AND PETER.` · `THEY WERE AFRAID, FOR.` · `TROMOS AND EKSTASIS.` · then, large: `HE IS RISEN; HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that ended, a job, a friendship, a season, a home, and remember what the women carried on that walk: the heaviness, the practical worries, who will roll away the stone. Then ask gently what began after that ending, even if you didn't see it at the time; you don't need a neat answer. If you pray, you can hold that ending before God.
Ekstasis, Greek for astonishment, being beside yourself. What seized the women at the empty tomb, paired with tromos, trembling.
Your line: he goes before you. The stone was rolled back before they arrived. Two hundred twenty-nine days now.

howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter and on Sundays; some churches hold sunrise services on Easter morning, and Orthodox Christians greet each other with Christ is risen, answered, truly he is risen.

what it means: the oldest copies end with the women fleeing an empty tomb, trembling and afraid.
what a scholar hears: the last Greek word is gar, for; scholars still debate whether Mark meant to stop there or the ending was lost.

chat.says: How does Mark's Gospel end? Doesn't Jesus appear to anyone?
options: In the oldest copies, the women flee the empty tomb trembling, and it stops.
Jesus himself rolls the stone away and greets Peter at the tomb.
The disciples find the tomb empty and preach to the whole city.
chat.meaning: In the oldest complete copies, Mark ends: they were afraid. No appearance, just trembling and astonishment, and the next step handed to the reader.

ekstasis.meaning: Greek for astonishment, being beside yourself

gar.meaning: Greek for for; Mark's last word

Salome.meaning: one of the three women at the tomb

sources.quoted: Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him.
And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid.

notes: The oldest complete manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, 4th century) end at 16:8. Confirm 'oldest copies'.
Mark 16:8 uses 'tromos kai ekstasis' ('trembling and astonishment'); KJV renders 'they trembled and were amazed'. The title follows the older rendering; confirm.
The debate (intended ending vs. lost ending) is presented without taking sides.
Tomorrow's day covers the longer ending (16:9–20); this day doesn't teach it.
